title: The Book of Ezekiel Timeline
sub: The Glory Departs, and Returns · Dry Bones Made Alive
desc: A priest-turned-prophet in exile sees the throne-chariot of God, acts out Jerusalem's siege in his own body, watches the glory of the LORD leave the temple gate by gate — then, on the far side of the city's fall, prophesies a valley of dry bones into a living army and the same glory back into a new temple forever.

eras.label: Era I · Ezekiel 1
eras.name: The Vision of the Divine Throne-Chariot
eras.dates: Exiled by the Kebar River, the priest Ezekiel sees a windstorm from the north resolve into four impossible living beings with wheels within wheels full of eyes, crowned by a throne of sapphire and a figure of amber and fire — the book's opening vision is so overwhelming that Ezekiel can only describe it in layered approximations, "something like" and "the appearance of."

events.title: Four Living Beings in a Windstorm From the North
events.detail: A priest among the exiles at the Kebar River sees the heavens open on an enormous storm cloud, resolving into four impossible living beings — each with four faces (man, lion, ox, eagle) and four wings, moving in any direction at once without ever turning.

verses.text: In the fire were what looked like four living beings. In their appearance they had human form, but each had four faces and four wings.

events.title: Wheels Within Wheels, and a Throne of Sapphire
events.detail: Wheels "full of eyes all around" move beside the living beings as if driven by a single shared spirit, and above it all, on a throne like sapphire, Ezekiel glimpses a form like a man wrapped in fire and rainbow light — the appearance, he says carefully, of the glory of the LORD, a vision so overwhelming he can only fall face down.

verses.text: like the appearance of a rainbow in the clouds after the rain. This was the appearance of the surrounding brilliant light; it looked like the glory of the LORD [Yahweh]. When I saw it, I threw myself face down, and I heard a voice speaking.

eras.label: Era II · Ezekiel 2-3
eras.name: Ezekiel Eats the Scroll, and Is Made a Watchman
eras.dates: Commissioned to speak to a nation he is told in advance will not listen, Ezekiel is handed a scroll covered on both sides with laments, mourning, and woe, and told to eat it — finding it strangely sweet as honey — before being appointed a watchman personally responsible for whether he sounds the warning, whatever the people do with it.

events.title: "Written on It Were Laments, Mourning, and Woe"
events.detail: Standing before a rebellious, hard-hearted people he is warned in advance will resist him, Ezekiel is handed a scroll covered front and back with nothing but grief — laments, mourning, and woe — the entire content of his coming ministry compressed into a single object.

events.title: "Sweet Like Honey in My Mouth"
events.detail: Told to eat the scroll of grief rather than merely read it, Ezekiel finds it unexpectedly sweet, before being told he is spared the harder task of preaching to a foreign nation with an unintelligible language — Israel's own people, who share his language, will still refuse to listen, because their resistance is really aimed at the LORD, not at him.

verses.text: "Son of man, feed your stomach and fill your belly with this scroll I am giving to you." So I ate it, and it was sweet like honey in my mouth.
"if I had sent you to them, they would listen to you! But the house of Israel is unwilling to listen to you, because they are not willing to listen to me."

events.title: Appointed a Watchman, and Struck Mute
events.detail: Ezekiel is personally held responsible for whether he sounds the warning trumpet, whatever the outcome — the watchman's job is to warn, not to guarantee obedience — before he is struck mute except when the LORD specifically gives him something to say, a silence that will govern much of what follows.

verses.text: "I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel… if you warn the wicked and he does not turn from his wicked deed… he will die for his iniquity but you will have saved your own life."

eras.label: Era III · Ezekiel 4-5
eras.name: Sign-Acts of the Siege: The Brick, the Iron Pan, and the Shaved Hair
eras.dates: Rather than simply preaching, Ezekiel is made to physically act out Jerusalem's coming siege — lying bound on his side for over a year eating rationed, defiled food, then shaving his head and dividing the hair into thirds to dramatize exactly how the city's population will be burned, killed, and scattered.

events.title: Lying on His Side for 430 Days, Eating Rationed Food
events.detail: Ezekiel inscribes Jerusalem on a clay brick, lays actual siege works against it as a model, then lies bound on his left side for 390 days and his right for 40 — one day for each year of Israel's and Judah's iniquity — eating meager, defiled rations to dramatize the coming famine.

verses.text: "lie on your left side and place the iniquity of the house of Israel on it. For the number of days you lie on your side you will bear their iniquity… 390 days… then lie down a second time, but on your right side, and bear the iniquity of the house of Judah 40 days."

events.title: Hair Shaved, Weighed, and Divided in Thirds
events.detail: Ezekiel shaves his head and beard with a sword, then divides the hair into three precise portions — burned inside the model city, slashed with a sword around it, and scattered to the wind — a living forecast of exactly how Jerusalem's population will die: by plague and famine, by the sword, and by scattering.

verses.text: A third of your people will die of plague or be overcome by the famine within you. A third of your people will fall by the sword surrounding you, and a third I will scatter to the winds.

eras.label: Era IV · Ezekiel 6-7
eras.name: Judgment on the Mountains of Israel, and "An End Has Come"
eras.dates: The high places scattered across Israel's mountains and hills are singled out for direct destruction, and the book's rhythmic, drumbeat refrain of finality — "an end! the end is coming!" — announces that all the ordinary structures of daily life, buying and selling, mourning and rejoicing, are about to become irrelevant.

events.title: Idols Shattered on Every High Hill
events.detail: The LORD addresses Israel's mountains, hills, ravines, and valleys directly, promising to scatter the corpses of idol-worshipers in front of the very idols they served, so that even a scattered, surviving remnant will finally "loathe themselves" for what they did.

verses.text: Then your survivors will remember me among the nations where they are exiled… They will loathe themselves because of the evil they have done.

events.title: "An End! The End Is Coming!"
events.detail: A rhythmic, hammering refrain announces total finality — the end, doom, the day — arriving so completely that ordinary economic life collapses: buyers will not celebrate and sellers will not mourn, because the property itself will not survive to change hands.

verses.text: "An end! The end is coming on the four corners of the land! The end is now upon you, and I will release my anger against you."

events.title: Silver and Gold Treated Like Filth
events.detail: Wealth itself becomes worthless overnight — silver discarded in the streets, gold "treated like filth" — since none of it can buy deliverance on the day of the LORD's fury, and even the nation's institutions of guidance collapse together: no vision from a prophet, no instruction from a priest, no counsel from an elder.

verses.text: They will discard their silver in the streets, and their gold will be treated like filth. Their silver and gold will not be able to deliver them on the day of the LORD's [Yahweh's] fury.

eras.label: Era V · Ezekiel 8-9
eras.name: Abominations in the Temple, and the Mark on the Forehead
eras.dates: Carried by vision to Jerusalem itself, Ezekiel is shown escalating scenes of idolatry hidden inside the LORD's own temple — culminating in elders worshiping in a secret chamber and men bowing to the sun with their backs to the sanctuary — before six executioners are sent through the city, sparing only those marked for their genuine grief over what has happened.

events.title: "You Will See Greater Abominations Than These"
events.detail: In a visionary journey to Jerusalem, Ezekiel is shown an escalating tour of idolatry hidden inside the LORD's own temple — a jealousy-provoking statue, seventy elders burning incense to wall-carved images in a secret chamber, women weeping for the god Tammuz, and finally men with their backs to the temple worshiping the rising sun.

verses.text: "Do you see, son of man, what the elders of the house of Israel are doing in the dark, each in the chamber of his idolatrous images? For they think, 'The LORD [Yahweh] does not see us! The LORD [Yahweh] has abandoned the land!'"

events.title: A Mark Spares the Grieving; Six Executioners Strike the Rest
events.detail: Before judgment falls, one man dressed in linen marks the foreheads of everyone who genuinely grieves over the city's abominations, and only those marked are spared when six armed executioners then sweep through Jerusalem, beginning deliberately at the temple itself.

verses.text: "Go through the city of Jerusalem and put a mark on the foreheads of the people who moan and groan over all the abominations practiced in it."

eras.label: Era VI · Ezekiel 10-11
eras.name: The Glory Departs the Temple, and a New Heart Promised
eras.dates: The same wheeled, many-eyed cherubim from chapter 1 reappear as the glory of the LORD deliberately relocates out of the temple and pauses over the mountain east of the city — a slow, staged departure — even as a startling promise of restoration follows immediately after: a new heart and a new spirit for the very people being judged.

events.title: The Glory of the LORD Departs, Cherub by Cherub
events.detail: The cherubim and their eye-covered wheelwork from chapter 1's vision reappear here explicitly identified as the same living beings, and the glory of the LORD moves deliberately — from above the cherub, to the temple threshold, to the east gate — a slow-motion, staged withdrawal rather than a sudden abandonment.

verses.text: Then the glory of the LORD [Yahweh] moved away from the threshold of the temple and stopped above the cherubim. The cherubim spread their wings, and they rose up from the earth.

events.title: "This City Is a Cooking Pot, and We Are the Meat"
events.detail: Confident officials plotting evil in the city dismiss danger with a callous proverb comparing Jerusalem to a protective cooking pot — a metaphor Ezekiel is told to invert completely, since the corpses they have already produced are the real meat, and they themselves will be dragged out of the pot to die at Israel's border.

verses.text: "The time is not near to build houses; the city is a cooking pot, and we are the meat in it."

events.title: "I Will Give You a New Heart"
events.detail: Even as judgment proceeds, the LORD promises to be "a little sanctuary" for the scattered exiles and to one day give them one heart and a new spirit, removing hearts of stone for hearts of flesh — the first appearance of a promise the book will return to more fully in chapter 36.

verses.text: "I will give them one heart and I will put a new spirit within them; I will remove the hearts of stone from their bodies and I will give them tender hearts, so that they may follow my statutes."

eras.label: Era VII · Ezekiel 12
eras.name: Ezekiel's Sign-Act of Exile
eras.dates: In broad daylight, Ezekiel packs his belongings, digs through a wall, and walks out covered and blind-seeming, all as a living rehearsal of exactly how Jerusalem's own prince will attempt to flee the city — a lesson delivered specifically to retire a popular proverb claiming prophecy always takes too long to matter.

events.title: Packing for Exile in Full View of the People
events.detail: Ezekiel digs through a wall and carries his belongings out at dusk with his face covered, publicly rehearsing exactly what King Zedekiah will do when Jerusalem falls — down to the detail that he will not see the land he is being taken to, since his eyes will be put out before he arrives.

verses.text: The prince who is among them will raise his belongings onto his shoulder in darkness… I will throw my net over him, and he will be caught in my snare. I will bring him to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans (but he will not see it).

events.title: "Every Vision Will Be Fulfilled"
events.detail: A popular proverb dismissing prophecy as perpetually delayed — "the days pass slowly, and every vision fails" — is retired outright, replaced by the LORD's flat promise that his word will no longer be pushed off into some indefinite future.

verses.text: "None of my words will be delayed any longer! The word I speak will come to pass, declares the Sovereign LORD [Adonai Yahweh]."

eras.label: Era VIII · Ezekiel 13
eras.name: False Prophets and Whitewashed Walls
eras.dates: Prophets who invent their own visions and claim the LORD's authority for them are compared to builders coating a flimsy, mortarless wall with whitewash to hide its weakness — a cosmetic fix the LORD promises to expose with hail, flood, and wind — while female prophets selling magic charms for handfuls of barley are condemned in equally concrete, specific terms.

events.title: Whitewash on a Wall Without Mortar
events.detail: Prophets "who prophesy from their imagination" are compared to builders slapping whitewash over a structurally unsound wall — cosmetic reassurance covering real weakness — a fraud the LORD promises to expose with a literal storm of hail and wind that will bring the whole thing crashing down.

verses.text: they have led my people astray saying, "All is well," when things are not well. When anyone builds a wall without mortar, they coat it with whitewash.
I will break down the wall you coated with whitewash and knock it to the ground so that its foundation is exposed.

events.title: Magic Charms for Handfuls of Barley
events.detail: Female prophets who sew magic wristbands and headbands to manipulate people's lives are condemned for profaning the LORD "for handfuls of barley and scraps of bread" — literally profiting off both the death of the innocent and the false security of the guilty.

eras.label: Era IX · Ezekiel 14
eras.name: Idols in the Heart, and Noah, Daniel, and Job
eras.dates: Elders who outwardly consult Ezekiel while secretly harboring idols "in their hearts" are told bluntly that even Noah, Daniel, and Job — three legendary examples of individual righteousness — could not save anyone but themselves once judgment against a land is fully decided.

events.title: Idols Erected "in Their Hearts"
events.detail: Elders who come to consult Ezekiel while privately harboring idolatry are told the LORD will "answer him personally" according to the enormity of that hidden idolatry — a warning that outward religious consultation cannot substitute for an undivided heart.

verses.text: "these men have erected their idols in their hearts and placed the obstacle leading to their iniquity right before their faces. Should I really allow them to seek me?"

events.title: Not Even Noah, Daniel, and Job Could Save the Nation
events.detail: In a striking hypothetical, the LORD names three legendary examples of personal righteousness — Noah, Daniel, and Job — and insists that even they, if present, could save only themselves and not their own children once judgment against a land is decided, a stark statement about the limits of vicarious righteousness.

verses.text: "Even if these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they would save only their own lives by their righteousness, declares the Sovereign LORD [Adonai Yahweh]."

eras.label: Era X · Ezekiel 15
eras.name: The Useless Wood of the Vine
eras.dates: A short, sharp parable notes that grapevine wood, unlike other trees, is useless for anything at all once cut from the vine — not even a peg to hang something on — making it a fitting image for Jerusalem, already burned at both ends and now destined for the fire completely.

events.title: Vine Wood: Useless Even Before It Burns
events.detail: Unlike other forest trees, vine wood cannot be made into anything useful even when whole, let alone once charred by fire on both ends — a deliberately unflattering image for Jerusalem, whose worth the LORD says was never in its wood but only in the fruit it was supposed to bear.

verses.text: It is thrown in the fire for fuel; when the fire has burned up both ends of it… will it be useful for anything? Indeed! If it was not made into anything useful when it was whole, how much less can it be made into anything when the fire has burned it up.

eras.label: Era XI · Ezekiel 16
eras.name: Jerusalem the Unfaithful Wife
eras.dates: In the book's longest single chapter, Jerusalem's history is retold as an abandoned newborn rescued and raised to royal beauty by the LORD himself, only to become a prostitute who paid her own lovers rather than the reverse — an allegory so raw it compares Jerusalem unfavorably to Sodom before closing, remarkably, on a promise of an everlasting covenant anyway.

events.title: An Abandoned Newborn Raised to Royalty
events.detail: Jerusalem's origin is retold as an unwanted infant left in an open field, umbilical cord uncut, rescued by the LORD's own passing command to "Live!" and raised through adolescence into a royal bride adorned with jewelry, fine linen, and a share in his own splendor.

verses.text: "I passed by you and saw you kicking around helplessly in your blood. I said to you as you lay there in your blood, 'Live!'"
"I spread my cloak over you and covered your nakedness. I swore a solemn oath to you and entered into a marriage covenant with you."

events.title: "You Trusted in Your Beauty" — Prostitution With Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon
events.detail: Rather than reciprocating the LORD's devotion, Jerusalem is described using her own God-given beauty and wealth to seduce foreign powers one after another — Egypt, Assyria, and finally Babylon — in a startling reversal of ordinary prostitution: she paid her lovers, rather than the other way around.

verses.text: "All prostitutes receive payment, but instead you give gifts to every one of your lovers… you became the opposite!"

events.title: "Your Sister Sodom Never Behaved as Wickedly as You"
events.detail: Judgment is announced in the graphic terms of an adulteress publicly exposed and stoned by a gathered mob, and the chapter delivers its most provocative comparison: Jerusalem's sins have actually outstripped those of the proverbial Sodom, making her own sister-cities look righteous by comparison.

verses.text: "your sister Sodom and her daughters never behaved as wickedly as you and your daughters have behaved… they had majesty, abundance of food, and enjoyed carefree ease, but they did not help the poor and needy."

events.title: An Everlasting Covenant, Despite Everything
events.detail: Astonishingly, the chapter's harshest indictment resolves into restoration for Sodom, Samaria, and Jerusalem alike, and a renewed, permanent covenant that the LORD will keep even though Jerusalem broke her original oath entirely.

verses.text: "I will remember the covenant I made with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish a lasting covenant with you."

eras.label: Era XII · Ezekiel 17
eras.name: The Riddle of Two Eagles and a Vine
eras.dates: A deliberately cryptic parable about a great eagle transplanting a cedar shoot, then a vine bending toward a second eagle instead, turns out to be recent political history in disguise — Nebuchadnezzar's installation and betrayal of King Zedekiah — before resolving into a genuinely messianic image of a tender twig planted on a high mountain by the LORD's own hand.

events.title: A Riddle: Two Eagles and a Vine
events.detail: A deliberately obscure parable describes a great eagle plucking the top of a cedar and planting a seedling instead, only for that seedling to grow into a vine that bends disloyally toward a second, rival eagle — a riddle the chapter does not explain until its second half.

events.title: The Riddle Decoded: Zedekiah's Betrayal, and a Messianic Sprig
events.detail: The riddle turns out to be recent history — Nebuchadnezzar installed Zedekiah under oath, and Zedekiah's secret appeal to Egypt for help is exposed as exactly the disloyal "bending toward the second eagle" the parable described — before the chapter closes on hope: the LORD himself will one day plant a tender twig from the cedar's top on a high mountain, where it will become a beautiful, sheltering tree.

verses.text: "I will take a sprig from the lofty top of the cedar and plant it… on a high and lofty mountain… it will raise branches and produce fruit and become a beautiful cedar. Every bird will live under it."

eras.label: Era XIII · Ezekiel 18
eras.name: Individual Responsibility: "The Soul Who Sins Will Die"
eras.dates: Answering a popular proverb blaming present suffering on ancestral sin, the LORD walks through three generations of a single family — a righteous father, a violent son, and a righteous grandson — to establish that each person answers only for their own conduct, closing with the striking claim that the LORD takes no pleasure at all in anyone's death.

events.title: Three Generations: A Righteous Father, a Violent Son, a Righteous Grandson
events.detail: Answering the popular complaint that children suffer for their parents' "sour grapes," the LORD walks through three consecutive generations of one family — righteous, then violent, then righteous again — to establish decisively that each person's fate depends entirely on their own conduct, not their ancestry.

verses.text: The person who sins is the one who will die. A son will not suffer for his father's iniquity, and a father will not suffer for his son's iniquity; the righteous person will be judged according to his righteousness and the wicked person according to his wickedness.

events.title: "I Take No Delight in the Death of the Wicked"
events.detail: Genuine repentance at any point erases the accumulated record of a wicked life entirely, and the chapter closes on one of the book's most tender statements about the character of God — he takes no pleasure whatsoever in anyone's death, and urges the nation directly: "repent and live!"

verses.text: "Do I actually delight in the death of the wicked, declares the Sovereign LORD [Adonai Yahweh]? Do I not prefer that he turn from his wicked conduct and live?"
"fashion yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why should you die, O house of Israel? For I take no delight in the death of anyone… Repent and live!"

eras.label: Era XIV · Ezekiel 19
eras.name: A Lament for the Princes of Israel
eras.dates: A funeral song mourns Judah's royal line under two linked images — a lioness whose cubs are captured and caged one after another, and a flourishing vine transplanted into the wilderness where its strongest branches wither — closing the first major section of the book on an unmistakable note of grief.

events.title: A Lioness's Cubs, and a Transplanted Vine
events.detail: In a formal funeral lament, Judah's mother is pictured as a lioness whose cubs — successive kings — are trapped and dragged off to Egypt and Babylon in turn, and as a thriving vine whose strong branches are burned and transplanted into a dry, thirsty wasteland with no scepter left to rule.

verses.text: A fire has gone out from its branch; it has consumed its shoot and its fruit. No strong branch was left in it, nor a scepter to rule.

eras.label: Era XV · Ezekiel 20
eras.name: A History of Rebellion, From Egypt to the Promised Land
eras.dates: Elders coming to inquire of the LORD are flatly refused before Ezekiel recounts Israel's entire history as one continuous cycle of rebellion — in Egypt, in the wilderness, and even after entering the land — a pattern the LORD says he restrained only "for the sake of my reputation," before promising a final regathering "on my holy mountain."

events.title: "I Will Not Allow You to Seek Me"
events.detail: Elders coming to consult the LORD are turned away outright, and Ezekiel is instructed to retell Israel's entire history as an unbroken pattern of rebellion — idolatry retained from Egypt, statutes rejected in the wilderness — restrained from complete destruction each time not because Israel deserved it, but "for the sake of my reputation" before the watching nations.

verses.text: "Are you coming to seek me? As surely as I live, I will not allow you to seek me, declares the Sovereign LORD [Adonai Yahweh]."
"I acted for the sake of my reputation, so that I would not be profaned before the nations among whom they lived."

events.title: A Future Regathering "On My Holy Mountain"
events.detail: Even while condemning ongoing child sacrifice and idolatry, the chapter turns toward a promised future regathering that will pass the people "under the shepherd's staff" into covenant discipline, ending with all Israel finally worshiping together on the LORD's holy mountain.

verses.text: "there on my holy mountain, the high mountain of Israel, declares the Sovereign LORD [Adonai Yahweh], all the house of Israel will serve me, all of them in the land."

eras.label: Era XVI · Ezekiel 21
eras.name: The Sword Song, and Nebuchadnezzar at the Crossroads
eras.dates: A chant-like poem pictures a sword sharpened and polished specifically for slaughter, cutting off "both the righteous and the wicked" indiscriminately, before the king of Babylon himself is shown consulting omens at a literal fork in the road to decide whether to march against Jerusalem or Rabbah — a mundane act of pagan divination the LORD claims as his own instrument regardless. This chapter is numbered several verses earlier in most English Bibles, since NET's own text marks its opening at what it calls 20:45.

events.title: Fire in the South
events.detail: A brief oracle against the Negev pictures a fire consuming every tree, green and dry alike, indiscriminately — provoking Ezekiel's own complaint that people dismiss his prophecies as merely clever wordplay. (Numbered 20:45-49 in most English translations.)

events.title: A Sword Sharpened for Slaughter
events.detail: A chant-like poem describes a sword sharpened and polished specifically to cut down both the righteous and the wicked without distinction, commanding Ezekiel himself to groan and strike his thigh in grief as a public sign of what is coming. (Numbered 21:1-17 in most English translations.)

verses.text: "A sword, a sword is sharpened and also polished. It is sharpened for slaughter; it is polished to flash like lightning!"

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar Consults Omens at the Crossroads
events.detail: The king of Babylon is shown literally standing at a fork in the road, shaking arrows and reading animal livers to decide between attacking Rabbah of the Ammonites or Jerusalem — a scene of pagan divination the LORD nonetheless claims as the very means by which his own judgment against Jerusalem's "profane and wicked prince" will be carried out. (Numbered 21:18-32 in most English translations.)

verses.text: the king of Babylon stands at the fork in the road at the head of the two routes. He looks for omens: He shakes arrows, he consults idols, he examines animal livers.

eras.label: Era XVII · Ezekiel 22
eras.name: The Bloody City, and No One to Stand in the Gap
eras.dates: Jerusalem is indicted on a specific list of social sins — bribery, incest, extortion, contempt for parents — compared to worthless slag left over after silver refining, before the LORD's search for even a single person willing to "stand in the gap" on the nation's behalf comes back with a devastating result: no one.

events.title: The Bloody City Indicted
events.detail: Jerusalem's guilt is itemized in specific, unflinching detail — leaders who shed blood, contempt for parents, oppression of foreigners and orphans, incest, and bribery — described collectively as a city whose reputation for "turmoil" has spread near and far.

events.title: "I Found No One to Stand in the Gap"
events.detail: Israel is compared to worthless slag skimmed off silver in a smelting furnace, and the chapter's most striking line comes at its close — the LORD searched specifically for one person willing to "stand in the gap" and intercede for the land, and found absolutely no one.

verses.text: "I looked for a man from among them who would repair the wall and stand in the gap before me on behalf of the land, so that I would not destroy it, but I found no one."

eras.label: Era XVIII · Ezekiel 23
eras.name: Oholah and Oholibah: Two Sisters' Adultery
eras.dates: A second extended sexual allegory, even more explicit than chapter 16, names Samaria and Jerusalem as two sisters — Oholah and Oholibah — whose shared history of political and religious "prostitution" with Assyria, Egypt, and Babylon leads the younger sister to drink from the very cup of judgment that destroyed the elder.

events.title: Two Sisters Named: Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem)
events.detail: Samaria and Jerusalem are named outright as two sisters whose shared history began with prostitution in Egypt and continued through lustful political entanglement with Assyrian officers and, later, painted images of Babylonian warriors — Oholah's affair with Assyria ending in her own violent destruction.

verses.text: Oholah was the name of the older and Oholibah the name of her younger sister… Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem.

events.title: "You Will Drink Your Sister's Cup"
events.detail: Having watched her older sister's downfall and learned nothing from it, Oholibah is condemned to drink the identical cup of horror and desolation her sister Samaria already drained — judgment applied with deliberate, matching symmetry.

verses.text: "You have followed the ways of your sister, so I will place her cup of judgment in your hand… You will drink your sister's deep and wide cup."

events.title: Shared Judgment for Both Sisters
events.detail: The chapter closes by naming both sisters' sins together — child sacrifice, temple desecration, and entertaining foreign lovers on a "magnificent couch" set with the LORD's own incense and oil — bringing their shared judgment to a single, unified conclusion.

eras.label: Era XIX · Ezekiel 24
eras.name: The Boiling Pot, and Ezekiel's Wife
eras.dates: On the exact day Babylon's siege of Jerusalem actually begins, Ezekiel delivers a parable of a corrupted cooking pot too far gone to be cleaned by ordinary means, before receiving the book's most personally costly command: his own wife will die that very evening, and he is forbidden to mourn her at all, becoming a living object lesson for the city's coming, unmourned devastation.

events.title: A Pot Whose Rot Cannot Be Removed
events.detail: On the precise day Babylon's siege of Jerusalem begins — a date Ezekiel is told to record exactly — a parable of a cooking pot filled with choice meat but ruined by embedded rot pictures a city so thoroughly corrupted that ordinary cleansing has become impossible.

verses.text: "Son of man, write down the name of this day, this very day. The king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem this very day."

events.title: "The Delight of Your Eyes" — Ezekiel's Wife Dies
events.detail: In the book's most personally costly sign-act, Ezekiel is told his own wife will die that evening and he is forbidden to perform any customary mourning rite at all — his suppressed grief becoming a living preview of how Jerusalem's own coming devastation will be too total even for ordinary mourning.

verses.text: "I am about to take the delight of your eyes away from you with a jolt, but you must not mourn or weep or shed tears."… my wife died in the evening. In the morning I acted just as I was commanded.

eras.label: Era XX · Ezekiel 25
eras.name: Oracles Against Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia
eras.dates: Four short oracles against Judah's immediate neighbors share a single common thread — each nation is condemned specifically for the malicious satisfaction it took in Jerusalem's fall, whether through mockery, exploitation, vengeance, or unrelenting hostility.

events.title: Ammon: Mocking Judgment on the Sanctuary
events.detail: Ammon's gloating "Aha!" over the desecration of the temple and Judah's exile is answered with the promise of becoming pasture for eastern nomads' camels and sheep, its capital reduced to grazing land.

events.title: Moab: "Judah Is Like All the Other Nations"
events.detail: Moab's dismissive comment that Judah's downfall proves it was never really special is answered by exposing Moab's own frontier cities, stripped of their border defenses and handed over to the same eastern tribes as Ammon.

events.title: Edom: Vengeance Repaid by Israel's Own Hand
events.detail: Edom, condemned specifically for exploiting Judah's weakness through active revenge rather than mere words, is promised that the LORD's own vengeance against it will be carried out through the hand of Israel itself.

events.title: Philistia: Unrelenting, Merciless Hostility
events.detail: The Philistines' "unrelenting hostility" toward Judah earns a matching promise of great vengeance, closing this short sequence of oracles on the same theme that unites all four: malice toward a neighbor in crisis draws the LORD's own direct response.

eras.label: Era XXI · Ezekiel 26
eras.name: Oracle Against Tyre
eras.dates: The great maritime trading city of Tyre, caught gloating over the economic opportunity Jerusalem's destruction represents, is promised a siege by "many nations" so total the city will be scraped down to bare rock — a fishing-net-drying rock where her once-famous harp music will fall permanently silent.

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar's Siege Foretold
events.detail: Tyre's gleeful expectation of inheriting Jerusalem's lost trade — "the gateway of the peoples is broken; it has swung open to me" — draws the promise of a specific siege by Nebuchadnezzar, complete with battering rams, siege ramps, and the eventual scraping of the city down to bare rock.

verses.text: "Tyre has said about Jerusalem, 'Aha, the gateway of the peoples is broken; it has swung open to me. I will become rich, now that she has been destroyed.'"

events.title: The Coastlands' Lament for a Sunken City
events.detail: Neighboring maritime princes are pictured trembling on the ground in shock at Tyre's downfall, singing a lament that pictures the once-renowned city vanished from the sea entirely — sought after, the LORD says, but never found again.

eras.label: Era XXII · Ezekiel 27
eras.name: A Lament for Tyre, the Great Trading Ship
eras.dates: An extended funeral song pictures Tyre itself as a magnificent ship built from the finest materials of the ancient world — Lebanese cedar, Egyptian linen, ivory and ebony — cataloging dozens of trading partners before the ship, loaded down with its own wealth, is wrecked by an east wind and sinks with everyone aboard.

events.title: "I Am Perfectly Beautiful" — Tyre Built Like a Ship
events.detail: Tyre's own self-praise as "perfectly beautiful" introduces an extended metaphor picturing the city as a magnificent ship, built from Senir fir, Lebanese cedar masts, and Bashan oak oars, crewed by skilled sailors from Sidon and Gebal.

events.title: A Catalog of Trading Partners
events.detail: An extraordinarily detailed inventory names dozens of Tyre's trading partners across the ancient world — Tarshish for silver, Judah and Israel for wheat and honey, Damascus for wine, Sheba for spices and gold — cataloging the sheer economic reach that made the city's coming fall so consequential.

events.title: Wrecked in the Heart of the Seas
events.detail: The ship-city, weighed down by its own accumulated wealth, is wrecked by an east wind and sinks with its entire crew, prompting the kings and traders who once profited from her to tear their hair and throw dust on their heads in genuine, horrified mourning.

verses.text: Now you are wrecked by the seas, in the depths of the waters; your merchandise and all your company have sunk along with you.

eras.label: Era XXIII · Ezekiel 28
eras.name: The Fall of the King of Tyre, Once in Eden
eras.dates: Tyre's own ruler is confronted first for claiming outright to be a god because of his wealth and wisdom, then addressed in even more elevated, mythic terms as a being once present in the garden of Eden itself, blameless until pride corrupted him — one of Scripture's most debated passages, closing with a shorter oracle against neighboring Sidon.

events.title: "I Am a God" — the Proud Prince of Tyre
events.detail: Tyre's ruler, credited with wisdom greater than the legendary Daniel and wealth amassed through trading skill, is condemned specifically for concluding from his own success that he is actually divine — a claim about to be disproven violently by ordinary foreign swords.

verses.text: "Your heart is proud and you said, 'I am a god; I sit in the seat of gods, in the heart of the seas'— yet you are a man and not a god, though you think you are godlike."

events.title: "You Were in Eden, the Garden of God"
events.detail: In language that has been read on multiple levels throughout history, the king of Tyre is addressed as a being once blameless, covered in precious stones, placed by an anointed guardian cherub on God's holy mountain — until pride "because of your beauty" corrupted him and he was cast out, consumed by a fire from within himself.

verses.text: "You were in Eden, the garden of God. Every precious stone was your covering… You were blameless in your behavior from the day you were created, until sin was discovered in you."

events.title: Oracle Against Sidon, and Israel's Promised Security
events.detail: A brief oracle against Tyre's neighbor Sidon closes this run of judgments, pivoting immediately into a promise that Israel will finally live securely on its own land, free from the surrounding "sharp briers" of its scornful neighbors.

eras.label: Era XXIV · Ezekiel 29-30
eras.name: Oracles Against Egypt: Pharaoh the Nile Monster, and Egypt's Allies Judged
eras.dates: Pharaoh, who claims personal ownership of the Nile as if he made it himself, is compared to a great river monster about to be hooked and hauled onto dry land to rot, while a wider oracle against Egypt's cities pictures the day of the LORD arriving specifically for a nation whose broken military "reed staff" once injured Israel's own hand for leaning on it.

events.title: Pharaoh the Nile Monster, Hooked and Left to Rot
events.detail: Pharaoh's boast that "my Nile is my own, I made it for myself" is answered by picturing him as a great river monster the LORD will hook through the jaws and drag onto open ground to rot unburied — a specific forty-year desolation for Egypt that ends not in annihilation but permanent insignificance.

verses.text: "Look, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great monster lying in the midst of its waterways, who has said, 'My Nile is my own, I made it for myself.'"

events.title: Egypt Given to Nebuchadnezzar as Unpaid Wages
events.detail: In an unusually concrete historical footnote, Egypt is assigned to Nebuchadnezzar's army as compensation for a grueling, unrewarded siege of Tyre — payment in conquered land for services already rendered elsewhere.

events.title: The Day of the LORD Against Egypt's Cities
events.detail: Named Egyptian cities — Memphis, Zoan, Thebes, Pelusium — are each singled out for specific destruction in a day-of-the-LORD oracle that recalls Egypt's own historical role as "a reed staff" whose broken support once tore Israel's shoulder for merely leaning on it.

verses.text: "Egypt's supporters will fall; her confident pride will crumble… They will be desolate among desolate lands."

events.title: Pharaoh's Arm Broken, Never to Heal
events.detail: The LORD describes Pharaoh's military arm as already broken and left unbandaged, unable to grip a sword ever again, while Nebuchadnezzar's own arm is deliberately strengthened — a direct, personal transfer of power from one king to the other.

eras.label: Era XXV · Ezekiel 31-32
eras.name: Egypt Compared to a Fallen Cedar, and a Lament for Pharaoh in Sheol
eras.dates: Pharaoh's greatness is compared to Assyria's own legendary, garden-of-Eden-rivaling cedar — felled for its arrogant height — before a final funeral lament pictures him descending to Sheol to join a grim company of previously fallen empires: Assyria, Elam, Edom, and the princes of the north, all lying uncircumcised among the slain.

events.title: Assyria's Fallen Cedar, a Warning for Egypt
events.detail: Rather than describing Egypt directly, the LORD holds up Assyria's own legendary, garden-of-Eden-rivaling cedar — envied by every tree in Eden itself — chopped down for growing proud of its height, as a direct warning of exactly what awaits Egypt for the same sin.

verses.text: "Because it was tall in stature, and its top reached into the clouds, and it was proud of its height, I gave it over to the leader of the nations."

events.title: A Lament for Pharaoh the Sea Monster
events.detail: A formal funeral song pictures Pharaoh's downfall darkening the sun, moon, and stars themselves, his flesh scattered across the mountains and valleys — grief expressed even by neighboring nations who shudder to imagine themselves facing the very fate about to overtake Egypt.

events.title: Pharaoh Joins the Uncircumcised Dead in Sheol
events.detail: In a grim underworld roll call, Pharaoh is welcomed into Sheol by a company of previously fallen powers already lying there — Assyria, Elam, Edom, and the princes of the north — each identified as "uncircumcised," killed by the sword, and bearing eternal shame among the dead.

verses.text: Pharaoh will see them and be consoled over all his hordes who were killed by the sword, Pharaoh and all his army, declares the Sovereign LORD [Adonai Yahweh].

eras.label: Era XXVI · Ezekiel 33
eras.name: The Watchman Renewed, and News of Jerusalem's Fall
eras.dates: The watchman commission from chapter 3 is restated in full, along with the book's clearest statement that repentance at any moment fully cancels a wicked record — right before a fugitive arrives from Jerusalem with the exact news the whole book has been building toward: the city has fallen.

events.title: The Watchman's Duty Restated
events.detail: The watchman metaphor returns in full, expanded with the book's clearest single statement of the doctrine already established in chapter 18 — a wicked person's sudden repentance cancels the record entirely, and a righteous person's sudden fall erases their prior credit just as completely.

verses.text: "As surely as I live, declares the Sovereign LORD [Adonai Yahweh], I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but prefer that the wicked change his behavior and live. Turn back, turn back from your evil deeds!"

events.title: "The City Has Been Defeated!"
events.detail: A fugitive finally arrives from Jerusalem with the news the entire book has been building toward since chapter 1 — the city has fallen — and Ezekiel's imposed muteness lifts at that exact moment, though the survivors still remaining in the ruined land continue making the same excuses about inherited land rights that doomed the city in the first place.

verses.text: "The city has been defeated!" … the LORD [Yahweh] opened my mouth and I was able to speak once more.

eras.label: Era XXVII · Ezekiel 34
eras.name: False Shepherds Condemned, and "My Servant David" the True Shepherd
eras.dates: Israel's failed rulers are indicted as shepherds who fed themselves rather than their flock, leaving the sheep scattered and prey to every wild animal — a failure the LORD answers by declaring he will personally search for his own scattered sheep, and appoint a single, permanent shepherd from David's own line to finally do the job right.

events.title: "Woe to the Shepherds Who Have Been Feeding Themselves"
events.detail: Israel's rulers are condemned in an extended shepherding metaphor for eating the fat and wearing the wool while leaving the actual sheep to wander unprotected — the direct cause, the LORD says, of the whole flock's scattering and exposure to wild predators.

verses.text: "Woe to the shepherds of Israel who have been feeding themselves! Should not shepherds feed the flock?… you have not strengthened the weak, healed the sick, bandaged the injured, brought back the strays, or sought the lost."

events.title: "I Myself Will Search for My Sheep" — My Servant David
events.detail: The LORD announces he will personally take over shepherding duties abandoned by Israel's rulers, actively seeking out the lost and scattered, before promising to install a single permanent shepherd from David's line — "my servant David" — under a covenant of peace that finally lets the flock live securely.

verses.text: "I myself will feed my sheep and I myself will make them lie down… I will seek the lost and bring back the strays; I will bandage the injured and strengthen the sick."
"I will set one shepherd over them, and he will feed them—namely, my servant David. He will feed them and will be their shepherd."

eras.label: Era XXVIII · Ezekiel 35-36
eras.name: Judgment on Mount Seir, and "I Will Give You a New Heart"
eras.dates: Edom's gloating over Israel's desolation is turned back on itself with matching desolation, before the book's most theologically consequential chapter promises the mountains of Israel will be repopulated and its people given a literal heart transplant — stone removed, flesh installed, and the LORD's own Spirit placed within them to finally make lasting obedience possible.

events.title: Edom's Gloating Answered With Matching Desolation
events.detail: Edom (Mount Seir), condemned for claiming Israel's abandoned mountains as its own spoils and hurling insults heard by the LORD personally, is promised the exact desolation it wished on its neighbor, delivered on the same terms it gave.

verses.text: "As you rejoiced over the inheritance of the house of Israel because it was desolate, so will I deal with you—you will be desolate, Mount Seir, and all Edom."

events.title: The Mountains of Israel Will Be Repopulated
events.detail: Directly addressed as if they were listening, Israel's own mountains — mocked and "devoured" by surrounding nations — are promised fresh population growth, rebuilt cities, and a permanent end to the insults they have endured.

events.title: "I Will Give You a New Heart, and I Will Put a New Spirit Within You"
events.detail: In the book's most theologically consequential passage, the LORD explains he acts not because Israel deserves it but for the sake of his own reputation among the nations, promising to sprinkle clean water, remove the heart of stone, install a heart of flesh, and place his own Spirit within the people so that obedience finally becomes possible rather than merely commanded.

verses.text: "I will give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will remove the heart of stone from your body and give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you."

eras.label: Era XXIX · Ezekiel 37
eras.name: The Valley of Dry Bones, and Two Sticks Made One
eras.dates: Set down in a valley littered with dry, hopeless bones, Ezekiel prophesies them into a living army — the book's most famous image of national resurrection — before a simpler sign-act joins two wooden sticks into one, dramatizing the eventual reunification of a divided Israel and Judah under a single shepherd-king from David's line.

events.title: "Can These Bones Live?" — the Valley of Dry Bones
events.detail: Set down in a valley of scattered, sun-bleached bones and asked whether they can possibly live, Ezekiel prophesies twice — first to the bones themselves, which reassemble with tendons and flesh, then to "breath" itself, which enters them and raises an entire living army, a direct answer to the exiles' own despairing complaint that their hope has perished.

verses.text: He said to me, "Son of man, can these bones live?" I said to him, "Sovereign LORD [Adonai Yahweh], you know." Then he said to me, "Prophesy over these bones."
"these bones are all the house of Israel. Look, they are saying, 'Our bones are dry, our hope has perished'… I am about to open your graves and will raise you from your graves, my people."

events.title: Two Sticks Made One — Judah and Israel Reunited
events.detail: In a simpler follow-up sign-act, two inscribed wooden sticks representing Judah and Israel are joined into a single piece in Ezekiel's hand, promising the two long-divided kingdoms will be permanently reunited under one king from David's line and an everlasting covenant of peace.

verses.text: "I will make them one nation in the land, on the mountains of Israel, and one king will rule over them all. They will never again be two nations and never again be divided into two kingdoms."

eras.label: Era XXX · Ezekiel 38-39
eras.name: Gog of Magog Defeated
eras.dates: In one of Scripture's most debated apocalyptic passages, a vast northern coalition led by Gog of Magog invades a peacefully resettled Israel with plunder on its mind, only to be destroyed so completely by earthquake, plague, and fire from heaven that the weapons alone fuel Israel's fires for seven years and the burial alone takes seven months.

events.title: Gog of Magog's Invasion Foretold
events.detail: A vast coalition led by Gog of Magog, joined by Persia, Cush, Put, and other northern allies, is drawn against a peacefully resettled Israel with plunder as its stated motive — an invasion the LORD claims responsibility for provoking, purely to display his own greatness before a watching world.

verses.text: "You will advance against my people Israel like a cloud covering the earth. In future days I will bring you against my land so that the nations may acknowledge me, when before their eyes I magnify myself through you, O Gog."

events.title: Gog's Defeat, and Israel's Final Restoration
events.detail: Gog's massive army is destroyed so completely that Israel burns nothing but captured enemy weapons for fuel for seven full years and spends seven months simply burying the dead to cleanse the land, closing the vision with a final promise that the LORD will never again hide his face from his regathered people.

verses.text: "I will no longer hide my face from them, when I pour out my Spirit on the house of Israel, declares the Sovereign LORD [Adonai Yahweh]."

eras.label: Era XXXI · Ezekiel 40-42
eras.name: The New Temple Measured
eras.dates: Fourteen years after Jerusalem's fall, Ezekiel is carried in vision to a very high mountain and handed over to a bronze-gleaming, measuring-rod-carrying guide who walks him gate by gate, chamber by chamber, through a temple complex rendered in more precise architectural detail than any other structure in the entire Bible.

events.title: Entering the Temple Complex: the East and North Gates
events.detail: Fourteen years after the city's fall, Ezekiel is set down on a high mountain and handed over to a bronze-gleaming guide with a measuring rod, who begins a methodical, gate-by-gate survey of an entirely new temple complex — its outer wall, its elaborate east gate with decorative palm trees, and its matching north gate.

verses.text: "Son of man, watch closely, listen carefully, and pay attention to everything I show you, for you have been brought here so that I can show it to you. Tell the house of Israel everything you see."

events.title: The South and Inner Gates, and the Sacrifice Tables
events.detail: The survey continues through matching south and inner-court gates, each built to identical specifications, before pausing at eight specific stone tables positioned for slaughtering burnt offerings — a level of architectural precision that runs through the entire nine-chapter vision.

events.title: The Sanctuary Itself Measured
events.detail: The measuring continues inward to the outer sanctuary, the inner sanctuary explicitly named "the Most Holy Place," and the surrounding side chambers, their walls carved throughout with alternating cherubim and palm trees.

verses.text: Then he measured its length as 35 feet and its width as 35 feet, before the outer sanctuary. He said to me, "This is the Most Holy Place."

events.title: The Priests' Chambers, and the Outer Wall
events.detail: The tour closes with the priests' holy chambers — where sacred garments must be changed before priests can rejoin ordinary people outside — and a final measurement of the entire complex's outer wall, built specifically "to separate the holy and common places."

verses.text: He measured it on all four sides. It had a wall around it… to separate the holy and common places.

eras.label: Era XXXII · Ezekiel 43-44
eras.name: The Glory Returns, and the Priesthood Restored
eras.dates: The same glory that departed the old temple in chapter 10 now returns to fill the new one from the east, and the LORD announces he will dwell there "forever" — before the priesthood itself is reorganized, with the Zadokite line restored to full service and the Levites who once strayed into idolatry given a diminished, supporting role instead.

events.title: The Glory of the LORD Returns to the Temple
events.detail: The same glory that slowly departed the old temple in chapter 10 now returns from the east with a sound "like that of rushing water," filling the new temple completely, and the LORD announces he will now dwell among his people "forever" — provided the recurring sins of royal idolatry and defilement are put away for good.

verses.text: The glory of the LORD [Yahweh] came into the temple by way of the gate that faces east… I watched the glory of the LORD [Yahweh] filling the temple.
"this is the place of my throne… where I will live among the people of Israel forever."

events.title: The Altar Measured and Consecrated
events.detail: Detailed measurements of the new altar's base, ledges, and horns are followed by a seven-day consecration ritual involving bulls and rams, after which the LORD promises to formally "accept" the people's offerings on the altar.

events.title: The Shut East Gate, and the Levites' Demotion
events.detail: The gate the LORD's glory entered through is permanently sealed shut, reserved only for the prince to use for ceremonial meals, while the Levites — condemned for once ministering to Israel's idols — are demoted from full priestly service to supporting temple duties as a consequence of their own past unfaithfulness.

verses.text: "This gate will be shut; it will not be opened, and no one will enter by it. For the LORD [Yahweh], the God of Israel, has entered by it; therefore it will remain shut."

events.title: The Zadokite Priests: Privileges and Restrictions
events.detail: The priestly line descended from Zadok, who stayed faithful "when the people of Israel went astray," is restored to full priestly service, bound by specific restrictions on dress, marriage, mourning, and diet designed to keep sacred and common life clearly distinguished.

verses.text: "the Levitical priests, the descendants of Zadok who kept the charge of my sanctuary when the people of Israel went astray from me, will approach me to minister to me."

eras.label: Era XXXIII · Ezekiel 45-46
eras.name: The Prince's Portion, and the Appointed Feasts
eras.dates: A holy allotment of land is set aside for the sanctuary, the priests, and the Levites, alongside honest weights and measures for everyone else, before detailed regulations for Passover and the regular daily offerings define exactly how the prince — a royal but explicitly non-priestly figure — is meant to lead worship in the new order.

events.title: A Holy Allotment, and Just Weights and Measures
events.detail: A precisely measured square of land is set apart for the sanctuary and the ministering priests, alongside separate portions for the Levites and the city itself, closing with a direct command to princes to stop their evictions and oppression and instead use honest, standardized weights and measures.

verses.text: "Enough, you princes of Israel! Put away violence and destruction and do what is just and right… You must use just balances, a just dry measure (an ephah), and a just liquid measure (a bath)."

events.title: Passover and the Appointed Feasts
events.detail: Detailed instructions for purifying the sanctuary at the year's start lead into regulations for the Passover festival, with the prince personally responsible for providing the sin offerings and burnt offerings on behalf of the whole nation.

events.title: The Sabbath, New Moon, and Daily Offerings
events.detail: Regular worship rhythms are established — the east gate opening specifically on Sabbaths and new moons for the prince's offerings, and a daily morning burnt offering that continues "perpetually," grounding the whole vision's grandeur in an unremarkable, repeating daily rhythm.

events.title: The Prince's Inheritance, and the Boiling Chambers
events.detail: Rules protecting the prince's land from being permanently transferred away from his own sons, together with practical kitchen facilities built into the temple's four corners for boiling sacrificial meat, close out the ritual regulations with attention to even the most mundane administrative details.

eras.label: Era XXXIV · Ezekiel 47
eras.name: The River Flowing From the Temple
eras.dates: Water trickling from beneath the temple threshold grows, measured stage by stage, into a river too deep to cross, freshening the Dead Sea itself into a thriving fishery and lining its banks with trees that bear fruit every month — one of Scripture's most vivid images of life flowing outward from the presence of God.

events.title: A River That Heals the Dead Sea
events.detail: Water trickling from under the temple threshold deepens with every measured stage — ankle, knee, waist, then a river too deep to cross — flowing east to freshen the notoriously dead, salty sea, filled with fish and lined by trees whose leaves never wither and whose fruit comes every month for food and healing.

verses.text: Every living creature that swarms where the river flows will live; there will be many fish… It will become fresh, and everything will live where the river flows.
every kind of tree will grow for food. Their leaves will not wither nor will their fruit fail, but they will bear fruit every month… Their fruit will be for food and their leaves for healing.

events.title: The Land's Borders, and Foreigners Included in the Inheritance
events.detail: The promised land's outer boundaries are mapped in specific geographic terms, closing with an unusually inclusive provision — resident foreigners who have settled and raised children in Israel are to receive a genuine tribal inheritance alongside native-born Israelites, not merely tolerated residency.

verses.text: "You must treat them as native-born among the people of Israel; they will be allotted an inheritance with you among the tribes of Israel."

eras.label: Era XXXV · Ezekiel 48
eras.name: The Land Allotted to the Twelve Tribes
eras.dates: The book's closing vision distributes the promised land in neat horizontal strips among the twelve tribes, sanctuary at the center, before naming the city's twelve gates after each tribe in turn and closing the entire book of Ezekiel on a single, resonant new name for the city itself.

events.title: Twelve Tribal Portions, North to South
events.detail: Each of the twelve tribes receives a horizontal strip of land running the full width of the country, arranged deliberately around a central holy allotment for the sanctuary, the priests, the Levites, and the city — geography organized entirely around the presence of God at its literal center.

events.title: The City's New Name: "The LORD Is There"
events.detail: The city's twelve gates are named for each of the twelve tribes in turn, and the entire book — which opened with a vision of the LORD's glory abandoning Jerusalem to judgment — closes on a single, deliberately chosen new name for the restored city that reverses that opening image completely.

verses.text: The circumference of the city will be 6 miles. The name of the city from that day forward will be: 'The LORD [Yahweh] Is There.'
